items.title: iv) Calculating Enthalpy Change of Formation of a substance (ΔHf°) using Enthalpy of Combustion and Enthalpies of Formation of other substances

source_refs.note: iv) Calculating Enthalpy Change of Formation of a substance (ΔHf°) using Enthalpy of Combustion and Enthalpies of Formation of other substances: a main subheading of 6.8 Hess's law of heat summation, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 128-128.

blocks.title: Sample problem 6.6
blocks.problem:
Propane (C₃H₈(g)) burns in oxygen according to the equation:
C₃H₈(g) + 5 O₂(g) → 3 CO₂(g) + 4 H₂O(g)
When 14.64 g of propane is burned in an excess of oxygen in a calorimeter at 25 °C and 1 atm pressure, 678.6 kJ of heat is evolved. Calculate the standard enthalpy of formation of propane. The standard enthalpies of formation of CO₂(g) and H₂O(g) are –393.51 kJ mol⁻¹ and –241.82 kJ mol⁻¹ respectively.
steps: Solution: The first step is to find the enthalpy change when one mole of propane is burned.
No. of moles of propane = 14.64/44.096 = 0.3320 mol
So, 0.3320 mol propane evolves heat = 678.6 kJ
1.0 mol propane evolves heat = 678.6/0.3320 kJ mol⁻¹ = –2044 kJ mol⁻¹
According to Hess’ law: ΔHr = [3 × ΔH°f (CO₂) + 4 × ΔH°f (H₂O)] – [1 × ΔH°c (C₃H₈) + 5 × ΔH°c (O₂)]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the Hess sum the reactant terms are enthalpies of formation, not of combustion: [1 × ΔH°f (C₃H₈) + 5 × ΔH°f (O₂)], and it is the enthalpy of formation of O₂(g) that is zero, because O₂ is an element in its standard state. Solving gives ΔH°f (C₃H₈) = –104 kJ mol⁻¹, as the book finds. The numbering is also a slip: the print has no Sample problem 6.5 and goes from 6.4 to 6.6; nothing is missing, so this is the fifth sample problem.
